He also asked about the intervention mechanisms that would be implemented should the government’s fiscal savings from the subsidies lead to higher prices for consumers. KPDN said more than 850 Price Monitoring Officers (PPH) were deployed daily to collect price data from over 2,000 business premises nationwide. The data was analysed to detect unreasonable price fluctuations and serve as an early warning mechanism. The ministry added that price information was also made available to consumers through the PriceCatcher application, enabling them to monitor prevailing market prices and make informed purchasing decisions. It said targeted fuel subsidies for the transport sector also served as a government intervention to curb leakages and misappropriations, while mitigating the impact of rising transportation costs on the prices of goods. KPDN said enforcement efforts had also been intensified to curb price manipulation and profiteering under the Price Control and Anti-Profiteering Act 2011 (Act 723). These include stepped-up monitoring and inspections to ensure that targeted fuel subsidies are not used as a pretext to increase the prices of goods, while safeguarding consumer interests. As part of its intervention measures, the ministry conducts a series of operations known as Ops Kesan whenever policy changes or economic developments could potentially affect the prices of goods and services. “Up to 2026, six series of Ops Kesan have been conducted, including Ops Kesan 2.0 following the implementation of targeted diesel subsidies and Ops Kesan 6.0 to address the risk of profiteering arising from global cost pressures. “Through these operations, KPDN monitors the entire supply chain and is empowered to issue written notices under Section 21 of Act 723 to examine changes in costs and profit margins. Legal action may be taken against parties found to have engaged in profiteering,” the ministry said. — Bernama
5f652bed411805f9: NOVEMBER 18 — Your next smartphone, cup of coffee or pair of sneakers may have travelled thousands of kilometres and passed through several countries before reaching you. That journey is becoming a growing headache for businesses. From trade wars and supply disruptions to rising fuel costs and carbon regulations, the global supply chains companies once took for granted are under pressure. And going green is increasingly becoming a matter of commercial survival, not environmental goodwill. The problem is that corporate promises have yet to translate into meaningful action. A recent MIT survey found that 83% of companies consider sustainability critical to their long-term success. Yet 68% admitted that tariff uncertainty had forced them to delay or abandon sustainability plans. Nearly a third said the disruptions had actually increased their emissions. In other words, sustainability is still one of the first casualties when business gets tough. That could prove costly. Research by FedEx found that 81% of consumers in Asia-Pacific prefer buying from companies that appear to operate sustainably, while nearly 40% are willing to pay more for environmentally friendly packaging. In Southeast Asia, more than half of small and medium businesses now factor sustainability into their supply chain decisions. Businesses may be tempted to put environmental commitments on hold when costs rise, but customers are not necessarily putting their expectations on hold with them. There is another misconception holding companies back: the idea that resilience and sustainability are competing priorities. They are not. Consider a company that depends on a single factory in one country and one type of fuel. A geopolitical crisis, sudden fuel price increase or new carbon tax could leave its entire operation exposed. Now consider a company with production spread across several regions, multiple suppliers and shorter transport routes. It is better positioned to withstand disruptions while reducing its environmental footprint. The same decisions can deliver two benefits: a more resilient business and a more sustainable supply chain. The World Economic Forum has declared the old “just-in-time” model dead. Companies that recognise this are already rethinking how their supply networks operate. Those that do not risk being caught off guard while continuing to squeeze suppliers for marginal cost savings. But rebuilding supply chains does not necessarily mean investing immediately in expensive new technology. Green logistics discussions often gravitate towards futuristic solutions such as hydrogen-powered trucks, electric ships and sustainable aviation fuel. These technologies matter, but businesses could be overlooking more immediate opportunities to cut emissions. MIT found that only 8% of freight fleets have fully switched to low-emission energy. Most still run on diesel. Waiting for every truck to become electric before making progress is unrealistic. There are ways to make existing fleets cleaner without replacing a single vehicle. Better route planning, consolidated loads and real-time tracking can help reduce unnecessary journeys and fuel consumption. The first priority should be knowing where emissions are coming from. Companies need systems that measure their carbon footprint across their entire supply chains, including emissions generated by suppliers. These typically account for more than 80% of a company's total footprint. Without that information, businesses are effectively trying to manage a problem they cannot see. Artificial intelligence can then help optimise delivery routes, cargo loads and warehouse energy consumption. FedEx, for instance, has developed tools that allow customers to see the carbon cost of individual shipments in real time. Technology, however, cannot compensate for a company that treats sustainability as somebody else's responsibility. MIT found that 57% of companies with dedicated cross-functional sustainability teams had integrated sustainability into their daily decisions. The figure fell to just 13% when responsibility was left to a single department. That gap points to a structural problem. Sustainability teams are often excluded from decisions that have the greatest long-term environmental consequences, such as where to build warehouses, which suppliers to engage for long-term contracts and how to design distribution networks. These decisions can lock in emissions for years. Yet only 33% of companies have board-level oversight of sustainability. When a crisis hits, there may be nobody senior enough to prevent environmental commitments from being sacrificed for short-term savings. Three things every business leader should know First, the winners will not necessarily be companies with the grandest sustainability pledges. They will be those that can demonstrate measurable progress and maintain it over time. Regulators increasingly want hard data, not glossy reports. Second, resilience and sustainability should not be treated as competing budget items. Regionalising production, diversifying suppliers and investing in digital planning tools can strengthen supply chains while reducing their environmental impact. Third, businesses need to be realistic about technology. Measure emissions first, make existing operations more efficient and only then consider replacing equipment. Buying expensive new technology without understanding where the biggest problems lie is unlikely to deliver the best returns. Ultimately, sustainability is no longer an optional extra that companies can showcase in their annual reports when business is doing well. Carbon has a price. Customers have expectations. Regulators are tightening scrutiny. And competitors are already finding ways to turn more sustainable operations into a commercial advantage. Companies that continue treating sustainability as a public relations exercise risk losing ground to those that recognise its value to their bottom line. The question is no longer whether businesses can afford to make their supply chains greener. It is whether they can afford not to. * The author is affiliated with the Tan Sri Omar Centre for STI Policy Studies at UCSI University and is an Adjunct Professor at the Ungku Aziz Centre for Development Studies, Universiti Malaya. He can be reached at ahmadibrahim@ucsiuniversity.edu.my. ** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
a8b50b5a87620c2c: JAKARTA: Indonesia's central bank announced a surprise interest rate hike Wednesday to bolster the rupiah as it sits around record lows against the dollar.

Bank Indonesia governor Destry Damayanti said the decision to lift borrowing costs 25 basis points to 6% was a "pre-emptive" measure to maintain inflation within policymakers' target range of 2.5-3.5%. Inflation is currently sitting at 3.2%.
"This increase is a step to further strengthen the stabilisation of the rupiah exchange rate from the impact of increasing global uncertainty," she told reporters in Jakarta.
The rupiah is Asia's worst-performing currency this year, and last week it hit 18,200 to the greenback, its weakest level on record.

The rate hike marked a "hawkish" turn by the central bank, wrote Bank Danamon Indonesia economist Irman Faiz in a note, with resilient domestic growth giving officials room for further monetary tightening.
"We expect another 25 basis-point hike in December to 6.25%, followed by a hold through 2027," he added.
"Markets pricing in a higher Fed rate path can keep US yields and the dollar elevated, adding to rupiah pressure."
Capital Economics said it expected two more 25-point hikes "given our view that further falls in the rupiah lie in store over the next twelve months".
"Failure to deliver would raise renewed concerns about the central bank’s credibility," it said.

61ee480c5f38c2a7: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has proposed that the concession for government vehicle supply be extended to other companies — categorised by vehicle type — to break the current monopoly held by a single concessionaire. PAC chairperson Datuk Wira Mas Ermieyati Samsudin said the categories that could be opened to other companies include vans, buses, four-wheel-drive vehicles, ambulances, and motorcycles. This was one of three additional recommendations by the PAC to improve the management of government concession vehicles, following the tabling of PAC’s Follow-Up Action Report on the Management of Government Vehicles under Concession Agreements in the Dewan Rakyat today. Mas Ermieyati added that the government must also finalise and enforce a supplementary agreement with Spanco Sdn Bhd to reduce vehicle leasing costs, as well as the excessive maintenance costs incurred when vehicles remain in use beyond their lease period. She noted that the PAC’s investigation into the management of government vehicles — under a 15-year concession agreement 2 between the Finance Ministry (MOF) and Spanco — revealed weaknesses in contract management and governance practices. This has led to delays in replacing vehicles that had reached the end of their lease terms. “The delay resulted in the government incurring additional costs for leasing and maintenance, while the imposition and collection of penalties for the delayed supply of vehicles were also slow. “Overall, the PAC is satisfied with the follow-up actions taken by MOF in implementing the recommendations outlined by the PAC,” she said in a statement today. The follow-up action report outlines MOF’s responses, along with PAC’s comments, regarding the actions taken on five key recommendations from the original report presented on July 9. The PAC also proposed expanding the supply concession to include vehicles intended for critical and rugged use — such as ambulances — to ensure that essential vehicles remain consistently available and can be replaced promptly in the event of a breakdown or accident. “The PAC further suggested that the government explore the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) to reduce reliance on fossil fuels, drive the development of the nation’s green technology industry, and attract foreign investment in this sector. It also calls on the government to prioritise data security and integrity when implementing the online system designed to manage and monitor concession vehicles,” she said. The PAC has also requested the government to ensure the system is fully accessible and functional in rural and remote areas, including in Sabah and Sarawak, Mas Ermieyati added. ad7ac4ab92a0752a: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 18 — Scandal-hit Californian chip giant Nvidia said yesterday it has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its “Hopper” series to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing’s access to powerful US semiconductors. Advanced Nvidia chips are the world’s top hardware for training and running AI tools — making them highly sensitive equipment in the tech race between Washington and Beijing. Lucrative sales of Nvidia chips — and allegations they are smuggled to China through third countries — are in the spotlight after former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman whom some US officials reportedly suspect of spying for Beijing. In the third quarter, “sales of licensed Hopper data centre products to China was $2.4 billion,” interim CEO Colette Kress told an earnings call Tuesday. But “our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China.” Kress did not give a reason for the decision. Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told AFP “the timing says quite a lot.” “We don’t know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first.” This year, the Trump administration began allowing limited sales of the flagship “H200” chip from Nvidia’s “Hopper” series to China. But US conditions have made it difficult for shipments to be approved, with Beijing also seen as reluctant to buy H200s as its homegrown chip industry gains momentum. Washington still bans the export of Nvidia’s even more advanced “Blackwell” and “Rubin” GPUs to China, citing security concerns as advanced AI has military applications. Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, a former director of a Singapore-based cloud computing company, has tanked Nvidia’s market value. Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, previously led Megaspeed International — a company under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese tech firms obtain Nvidia chips in violation of US export controls. As the scandal deepens, the United States moved Monday to close loopholes in those restrictions. Its new rules aim to crack down on both chip smuggling to China and the large gray market of Chinese companies renting computing power from data centres full of high-end Nvidia chips in Southeast Asian countries. 5ceffd59edda16a3: I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology.
A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage.

To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements.

Yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do.
That’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes.

Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages.
I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done.

But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements.

If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity.
Thinks of this as a distributed denial of satisfaction attack signaling that Microsoft can't solve this particular outage with a glib apology and a blog post. ®

61df821019c60e9d: NOVEMBER 18 — Have you ever walked into a room and forgotten why you went there? Or searched frantically for your phone, only to discover it was already in your hand? For many mothers, such moments are all too familiar. Society has even given them a name: “mum brain”. The expression is often used jokingly to describe the forgetfulness, mental fog and difficulty concentrating that some women experience during pregnancy and after childbirth. But what if motherhood is not simply making women more forgetful? What if the maternal brain is undergoing an extraordinary process of adaptation? Scientists are increasingly exploring this possibility, offering a different perspective on what happens to a woman’s brain when she becomes a mother. Motherhood is a major brain transition Researchers describe the psychological, physical and neurological transition into motherhood as matrescence. Much like adolescence, when the brain undergoes significant changes in preparation for adulthood, matrescence involves adaptations that help women navigate the demands of motherhood. A scientific review published in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2023 by Edwina Orchard and colleagues highlighted motherhood as an important period of brain development, with possible implications extending into later life. Consider the daily responsibilities of caring for a newborn. A mother must recognise different cries, remember feeding schedules, monitor her baby’s health, respond to emotional signals and make countless decisions, often while surviving on interrupted sleep. Her brain is constantly processing information, adjusting priorities and responding to unfamiliar situations. Rather than viewing every moment of forgetfulness as evidence of declining mental ability, researchers suggest we should recognise the enormous cognitive demands associated with motherhood. Is ‘mum brain’ really a decline in intelligence? Research suggests that pregnancy may be associated with small changes in certain aspects of memory. However, cognitive performance generally remains within normal limits. Interestingly, although many mothers report forgetfulness after childbirth, studies often find little corresponding impairment in formal cognitive assessments. This does not mean their experiences are imaginary. Sleep deprivation, emotional stress, hormonal changes and the continuous responsibility of caring for a child can affect concentration and everyday memory. A mother who forgets where she placed her keys may not have a less capable brain. She may simply be managing more responsibilities than her mind can comfortably accommodate. Importantly, these changes should never be interpreted as evidence that mothers are less intelligent or less capable professionally. Could motherhood benefit the ageing brain? One intriguing area of research concerns the possible long-term effects of motherhood on brain health. Scientists are investigating whether the complex mental and emotional demands of parenting may contribute to what is known as cognitive reserve. Cognitive reserve refers to the brain’s ability to maintain functioning despite ageing or neurological changes. Imagine a city with several alternative roads. When one route becomes blocked, traffic can continue through another. Similarly, a brain with greater cognitive reserve may be better equipped to compensate for certain age-related changes. Some studies have reported associations between motherhood and favourable patterns of cognitive functioning or brain structure later in life. However, these findings remain preliminary and sometimes inconsistent. Motherhood has not been proven to prevent dementia, and having more children does not necessarily produce better cognitive health. Nevertheless, this emerging research challenges the outdated assumption that motherhood only places limitations on women’s mental abilities. What Malaysian traditions can teach us In Malaysia, the importance of supporting mothers after childbirth has long been recognised through traditional confinement practices, commonly known as pantang. Across different communities, these practices often emphasise rest, recovery, nutritious meals and assistance from family members. Although certain traditional treatments lack strong scientific evidence, the underlying principle of allowing mothers time to recover deserves attention. Research examining traditional postnatal care has highlighted the importance of family support, companionship and opportunities for rest, while also recognising that restrictive practices can sometimes create additional stress. Modern science has not established that confinement improves maternal brain development. However, the emphasis on practical assistance offers a valuable lesson: mothers should not be expected to manage every responsibility alone. Supporting mothers means supporting their brains Too often, society celebrates mothers for their ability to multitask while overlooking the physical and emotional exhaustion behind that achievement. If motherhood encourages brain adaptation, it does not mean mothers should be burdened with even more responsibilities. Partners must share childcare and household duties. Employers should provide family-friendly working arrangements, while healthcare professionals should take concerns about memory, sleep and emotional wellbeing seriously. Above all, mothers need understanding rather than criticism. The next time a mother forgets something, perhaps we should reconsider the familiar joke about “mum brain”. She may be exhausted, overwhelmed or adjusting to one of life’s most demanding transitions. For generations, scientists have studied how mothers shape their children’s developing brains. Perhaps it is time we paid equal attention to how motherhood shapes the brains of mothers themselves. Motherhood does not simply change a woman’s life. It may also reshape how her brain adapts to the world. * Dr. Nor Shuhada Murad @ Mansor author is a Senior Lecturer and Cognitive Psychology Researcher at the Tun Abdullah Ahmad Badawi Cancer Centre (PKTAAB). ** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
17c2e30e15d669a6: SINGAPORE: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, plans to expand into five Asian markets next year with South and Southeast Asia as key priorities, its regional business head said, not long after the firm was hit with a record US$6.3 billion digital heist last month.

"We have ongoing conversations with at least five or six markets ... three of which are in quite mature stages," SB Seker told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday. "The others are ongoing conversations."

He did not specify the new markets that Binance, which currently has operating licences in more than 10 jurisdictions, was looking at, but said details of the planned expansion were expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of next year.
Binance's expansion plans come on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in US$6.3 billion being stolen from its platform last month.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, but Pyongyang has denied that.

The company, which resumed withdrawals in phases earlier this month after covering 95% of the lost tokens, said last weekend it aimed to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week.
The Binance heist, which has been described by experts as the largest crypto theft ever, has renewed scrutiny of inconsistent security practices in the industry.

Seker, the firm's head of APAC, said Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded.
"Think of all the financial services regulators and markets where we are present," he said, adding that there was no one country that led the charge in the investigations.
Binance says the Abu Dhabi Global Market's Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator.
Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry.

"The conversations now are 'well, this is an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat, and how does an entire ecosystem prepare for this?' It's moved away from the original incident to a much broader conversation," he said.
"We are part of the conversation, but we are not driving the conversation in isolation anymore."

7933e682ad2b584d: LONDON: British annual inflation rose to a one-year high of 3.6% in October from 3.5% in September, official figures showed on Wednesday, after the Bank of England raised interest rates earlier this month for the first time in three years.

The increase was in line with economists' median prediction in a Reuters poll, while the BoE earlier this month forecast 3.7% and sees nearly 5% inflation in the second quarter of 2027 due to higher energy prices caused by the Iran war.

The BoE was the slowest major advanced central bank to raise interest rates in response to the Iran war, having initially judged that cancelling previous plans to cut rates this year would be sufficient to keep inflation in check.

But now financial markets see a 90% chance that it will raise rates again in December and price in two or three more rate hikes for 2027 – a prospect which the BoE's chief economist, Huw Pill, described last week as "not outrageous".
Core consumer price inflation – which excludes volatile energy, food, alcohol and tobacco prices – held at 2.8% as economists had expected.
The services component of CPI – which some policymakers view as a better underlying gauge of price trends – also held at an unchanged rate of 3.7%, below the Reuters poll forecast of a rise to 3.8%.
Sterling fell slightly after the data.

Britain is highly exposed to the cost of imported natural gas for heating and electricity, and regulation which delays the impact of price rises on household bills means British inflation tends to be later to rise and fall than elsewhere.

BoE governor Andrew Bailey said a drop in international energy prices at the start of the month had largely come too late to stop a roughly 20% rise in regulated household energy bills due to take effect in January.

So far there have been few signs of the BoE's biggest fear, "second-round" effects, where wages and non-energy prices increase as workers and businesses try to offset losses caused by higher energy prices.
But when they voted to raise rates, BoE officials judged this was probably just a matter of time given how long oil prices have spent at or above US$100 a barrel.

145d6d67c25e21a7: Shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet. Electric automobiles cruise silently, chased by hushed flocks of electric scooters.

When I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed. That's not to say interest in the topic is low, but I didn't perceive any anxious artificial-general-intelligence-is-coming-and-will-destroy-us vibe.

The only conference talk that referenced AGI came from Ying Yang, a neuroscience PhD and serious influencer who has over 3.4 million followers on Chinese micro-blogging service Weibo, who enthused about the marketing and product development opportunities opening up to those who prepare for what’s coming.
AGI isn't P(doom) for the Chinese AI practitioners I met; it's a great new marketing tool.
Some of this may be due to the fact that the major US model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are effectively inaccessible on the Chinese side of the Great Firewall.
Engineers in China use DeepSeek or Kimi or GLM or MiniMax or MiMo or Qwen, all of which are now more than good enough for almost any task, and all offered without reference to The Terminator.

That's not to say that Chinese engineers and designers aren't facing the same crisis of self-worth we've seen elsewhere. A spectacular keynote from Ryo Lu asked, "When we can do anything, do we still know what we want?" Are our measures of self-worth pointless when we can no longer prove who we are by how many lines of code we've written, or frameworks we've designed?
Ryo landed on a line I'm hearing more frequently: "I want to build tools to help me be more and more involved, not prove that I'm needed less and less."
What followed showed just how good that tooling has become and what an AI engineer can do with it.

I saw an impressive demo from AutoArk of a 35 billion-parameter model running in just 2.5GB of smartphone RAM on an iPhone 16 Pro. DYNA's Zhong Shen showed how it builds robot hardware that will work with AI models updating every month.
My favorite presentation came from a bottle cap manufacturer called named Zhu Shihui, who reminded everyone in the audience that “the last mile is half the journey.”

Zhu flayed the class of consultants who never realize some manufacturing equipment is pre-digital but still insist every process can be easily automated. Never mind that workers in those factories lack deep digital skills (Zhu's average employee is in their late 40s) and that companies of this sort operate on margins so thin that resources simply aren't available to mount a complete transformation. Instead of swinging in on an AI wrecking ball, Zhu suggested the best approach is to exercise humility by seeking out an organization's tacit knowledge and using that as the basis for transformation.

Not long after Zhu left the podium, one of my Australian fellow travelers noted the significant proportion of women at the conference. I hadn't noticed, because having equal numbers of men and women at an engineering conference felt perfectly normal. Yet it's not something I've ever experienced at AI events in Australia or America. Whatever else the Chinese are doing with AI, they've put gender politics aside in AI engineering.

To put that in context: not long after leaving Shanghai, Alice Huang became major global news. A Shanghainese woman working in AI might look suspicious to an American who only ever sees men working in the field. Fei-Fei Li, Mira Murati and Daniela Amodei stand out as exceptions that prove the rule, but none of them, despite stellar work, have anywhere near the profiles of their male peers. In China, it's different.

It's become commonplace to be dismissive of Chinese progress in AI, ascribing it to copying, "distillation" and outright theft. Yet the Chinese make both the best small models and the best robots, and are moving ever-closer to making them work well together.

Chinese labs share their results with their peers and their competitors: nearly every model, closed or open, has benefited from the research done by DeepSeek and Alibaba. Practicality, balance and openness seem to be serving them well. Perhaps, after OpenAI follows Anthropic out to the public markets, and shareholders get a voice, stability, sanity and a bit of quiet will cross the Pacific. Those are some Chinese imports I'm looking forward to. ®

21edc08c543f7bee: Chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor. Now, the European Commission has made a preliminary finding that the company also runs a low-quality compliance regime that means it’s not meeting its regulatory obligations.

The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform.
Temu is a marketplace that allows third parties to sell on its platform, a model that doesn’t relieve it of responsibility for the goods available on its site and apps.
Eurocrats therefore have beef with Temu over several matters, including:
Requiring sellers who use the platform to test the quality of “only a very small share of products,” and then often not bothering to check the reports;
Not doing enough to prioritize checks of products in known high risk categories, like toys and cosmetics, then not following up on those checks;
Running a moderation system that mostly considers whether products comply with Temu’s terms and conditions, rather than product safety;
Not hiring enough human moderators to keep pace with growth in listings on Temu;
When it finds stores selling non-compliant goods, Temu acts against that store – but not the trader who may sell the same products in multiple stores;
Allowing stores to commit many serious infringements, including selling products that fail safety checks, before suspending their stores.
A Temu spokesperson told The Register the company respectfully disagrees with the EC's findings.

"Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products," the spokesperson said. "We will review and respond to the preliminary findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the Commission. We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns."
The EC has already tangled with Temu. In 2024 Eurocrats investigated its risk assessment processes. In May 2026, Eurocrats found Temu’s processes inadequate and levied a €200 million fine.
Brussels also sent a €550 million fine to another Chinese e-tailer, Alibaba, for not doing enough to stop the sale of dangerous goods.

This announcement of new action against Temu invoked Article 35 of the Digital Services Act, the sweeping regulation of online businesses under which the EU could fine Temu up to six percent of its global revenue and order corrective actions.

Europe is concerned that the low prices Chinese e-tailers charge are enabled by forced labor and ignoring dangerous products. EC officials believe those practices mean the likes of Temu don’t compete on a level playing field with continental retailers. The bloc has tried to make life harder for Chinese e-commerce outfits by charging a temporary €3 customs duty for every shipment sent from outside the EU and valued at under €150. Google recently revealed that new charge saw its advertising revenue from Asian customers fall.

Beijing sees its e-tail giants Temu, Shein, and Alibaba as important actors in its strategy to grow China’s exports and overall economy, which hasn’t performed strongly in recent years. Indeed, Chinese consumers have slowed their discretionary spending to the extent that Beijing last year subsidized purchases of consumer electronics – including Apple products – to keep cash registers ticking over. ®

e7bb5cbcc3bc3bfa: <!--kg-card-end: html--> A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion.

Gallup’s study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries.

A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.

Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. “Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all,” the researchers wrote.

Most of the respondents (82%) said they’d used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, “although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships,” they wrote.

The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as “high quality” and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: “In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating.”

People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. “However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships,” the researchers wrote.

The researchers also asked young people what they do online all day and the overwhelming majority (72%) said they spend their time scrolling short form content, mostly TikTok and Instagram. It’s also how they deal with loneliness, with six in 10 young people participating in this study reporting that they often or always scroll through online content when lonely.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> They also said scrolling works to dispel loneliness almost equally as well as hanging out with a friend in real life: “Although scrolling is more commonly used when young people feel lonely, those who use scrolling or in-person time as coping strategies report nearly identical levels of perceived helpfulness.”

Still, people who reported strong in-person friendships said they felt lonely less often, while online friendships have the same effect on loneliness regardless of how participants ranked the quality of those friendships. “No comparable difference appears across levels of online-only friendship quality,” the authors wrote. Having in-person relationships seemed to be what mattered most: “Higher loneliness is also more common among young people who frequently communicate online with strangers or online-only friends than among those who frequently communicate with in-person friends or family members.”

The relationships between loneliness, online friendships, and AI is complex and a person’s material conditions shape how they form friendships more than their access to a chatbot or how they use social media. The researchers’ analysis of young people who said they have no trusted adults in their lives makes that clear.

“Further analysis identifies several characteristics associated with having none of these friendship modes, but one stands out in particular: not having a trusted adult outside the family,” the researchers wrote. “This association remains substantial after accounting for country or residence, gender, age, urbanicity, and parent/ caregiver relationship quality.”

The study’s authors warned about reading too much into these results. “These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive,” they wrote. In general, people don’t have the same expectations of a chatbot that they do someone they know in real life.

“The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people’s relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly,” the study concluded.

461a1fe87414da12: A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector.  Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs. In a new paper, the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes. They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch. In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy. This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud. “There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Duping the detectors The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human. But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift. Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference.  However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text.  For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated. The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector. “After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren. The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector resilient to these distribution shifts. Adaptation in action In TTA, instead of freezing the model so it can’t change during deployment, researchers allow that model to adapt itself to incoming data after it has been released. For an AI text detector, these data are new pieces of text uploaded by users.  These data are unlabeled, so the detector developers don’t know which data were written by humans versus AI models. But these new data represent contemporary human and AI writing — exactly what the developers want the model to be able to predict.  With enough examples, the detector learns to identify patterns to determine which data are AI-generated and which are human-generated. The researchers studied TTA by creating datasets to contain a certain amount of AI-generated and human-generated text, but they don’t provide those labels to the model. They also used LLMs to generate some examples that resemble text written by AI to specifically evade a detector.  Then they performed the TTA training process and tested the model on ground-truth data. In experiments designed to mimic the natural shift in human language over time, a detector that used TTA was 85 percent accurate, while traditional methods only achieved 73 percent accuracy. And when it came to writing designed to thwart detection tools, existing methods could only identify about 27 percent, while TTA enabled the model to catch more than 93 percent of disguised text. “TTA has the potential to really help deployed AI-detection models in terms of being able to proactively address this iterative ‘gaming’ behavior by adversarial AI users,” Ren says. Adapting to shifts in human writing behavior is a more difficult TTA problem, since the shifts are slower and occur in more subtle ways, he adds. The researchers caution that TTA may not always be an effective solution as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and it becomes harder to find verifiable human text to use for training. “It isn’t entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,” Raghavan says. “There are some big, open questions about how you should think about science, writing, and art in a world where it is infeasible to tell the difference between human-generated content and AI content.” In the future, the researchers want to explore similar strategic domains where TTA could be useful and build better benchmarking tools to help engineers improve these AI detection models in a dynamic fashion. This project used API credits provided by Pangram to use their AI text detectors.

9a1b1cc4ad9efb0b: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).
Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November, which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products.
Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938, which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning.

The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes.

By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE.
Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw, says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder.

“Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.”

“We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:”
Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10.
Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.”

“Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.”

Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled.

“These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised.

Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled.
Akamai’s Chief Information Security Architect Jan Schaumann, writing on the Openwall project’s mailing list, expressed a little discomfort with Calif’s work.

“Calif.io set their priorities on publicity-maxxing, it seems,” he wrote, pointing out that the flaw-finding firm’s announcement of Java4Shell opens by stating “After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.”

Talos’s analysis of Java4Shell includes the interesting observation that it “has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.”
That second sentence perhaps supports Calif’s assertion that news of the flaw leaked before disclosure.
The rest of Big Red’s flaws
Java4Shell deserves a place high up on patch priority lists.

So do the six 10.10 flaws Oracle reported, three in its Access Manager product, one in the Oracle Platform Security for Java, another in the WebLogic Server, and one in Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition.
Big Red also repaired five 9.9-rated bugs, in Oracle Text, Hyperion, RDBMS, and Autovue.
The November patch dump also includes 28 flaws rated 9.8/10.
By Tenable Security’s count, 249 of the patches are for high severity bugs. Oracle’s Hyperion enterprise performance management accounts for 267 of the bugs.
Such is life in the age of AI-powered flaw finders – which Calif says burned through just $200 worth of tokens to find Java4Shell. ®
0dc4f489d775ec41: Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump are meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. The meeting is no doubt unusual – a very rare opportunity for the leaders of the world’s three major powers to exchange views directly on major global issues. It’s drawn comparisons to the Yalta conference of 1945, when US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian leader Joseph Stalin met to divide the world into spheres of influence after the second world war. But this is no Yalta 2.0. Nor is the Shenzhen summit an isolated episode. In May this year, Xi hosted back-to-back visits by Trump and Putin to Beijing. Trump reciprocated by hosting Xi in Washington in September, and met with Putin in Alaska last year. Taken together, these developments signal a broader shift away from the post-Cold War emphasis on global institutions and multilateral consultations toward a more personalised form of great power management. This is likely the new normal: a world in which China, Russia and the US act as an informal steering committee for global affairs, with Europe and other middle powers increasingly on the sidelines. Who’s invited into the room While China, Russia and the US remain strategic competitors, they increasingly share an understanding of how international politics should be conducted: less through institutions and coalitions, and more through direct engagement among a small number of major powers. This is by no means a formal alliance – not even between China and Russia – or a coordinated redesign of the international system. Rather, it reflects a common instinct toward great-power management of international affairs. All three favour a world in which major powers enjoy special rights and a privileged voice in shaping outcomes, negotiating major questions directly while limiting others’ involvement. Whether discussing war, security issues or economic stability, the major powers increasingly appear willing to bypass institutional channels in favour of high-level, direct diplomacy. For instance, Russia and the US just concluded a third round of peace talks this year in Abu Dhabi towards ending the Ukraine war. While Ukraine was part of the discussions, European negotiators were not. In such a world, power determines not only outcomes, but who gets invited into the room when outcomes are being discussed. Europe increasingly on the sidelines The most obvious casualty of this trend is Europe. During the Abu Dhabi talks last week, the Russian delegation made clear it wanted a new security framework for Europe modelled after the spheres of influence that existed during the Cold War. Trump has also flagged this as a possibility, saying the US was working on a big deal to end the war that would include “all of Europe”. After the talks, US special envoy Jared Kushner said Washington wanted Europe to be part of the process. He added, however, that finding someone who could credibly speak for Europe might be harder than persuading Russia to include them – a provocative statement. These comments have set off alarm bells in Europe and reinforced a growing perception that Europe is increasingly fragmented and marginalised as an actor in global politics. More significant, however, is that Xi ultimately agreed to join the Shenzhen trilateral summit. Having seen Europe sidelined from the Abu Dhabi talks, his decision to meet with Trump and Putin risked legitimising that exclusion, even if Ukraine is not on the agenda. That looks awkward for China, given Xi’s repeated emphasis on multipolarity and criticism of Cold War-style politics dominated by a few major powers. Beijing has also previously stressed that Europe should be “at the table” for Ukraine discussions. And yet Xi has agreed to meet with Trump and Putin. Moreover, China’s Foreign Ministry described the summit as having “groundbreaking significance”. The three leaders would “exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations,” it said. This suggests Beijing accepts a model of diplomacy centred on major powers, to the exclusion of others. And this creates an uncomfortable reality for Europe. Europe remains one of the world’s largest economic and technological centres, but it struggles to translate that weight into a unified strategic voice that carries weight on the global stage. The symbolism of the Shenzhen meeting is telling. Three leaders will be discussing issues that affect Europe’s future. And again, Europe itself will not be present. The middle powers’ counter-agenda However, the return of great-power diplomacy does not mean middle powers are irrelevant. European nations, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, and key Southeast Asian nations may not have the military capabilities or geopolitical heft to alter the distribution of power in the international system. But they do still have institutions, networks and coalitions. They can help shape international rules, sustain institutions and build partnerships capable of constraining larger states. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s call for closer middle-power cooperation reflects this logic. Rather than choosing sides in the great-power rivalry, he’s recognised the necessity to “stop pretending, to name the reality” while “building coalitions that work – issue by issue, with partners who share enough common ground to act together.” The more global power becomes concentrated in the hands of a few leaders, the stronger the incentive for middle powers to work together. They are unlikely to decide the overall direction of the world order, but they can still influence the rules, norms and institutions through which that order operates. The question raised by Shenzhen, therefore, is not whether a handful of major powers will continue to exercise disproportionate influence. They will. Rather, it is how the rest of the world will respond. 4510621dd9db4cda: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.
b17ffa7e6c38b2e0: ‘…stability, where it exists, is only ever twelve months deep’
Originally published on Global Voices

Activists hold a candlelight vigil to commemorate those who lost their lives in post-election violence in Tanzania in Nairobi, Kenya, on November 20, 2025. Image by Anadolu Lucas-Mukasa courtesy of FORUS.
By Clarisse Sih, Bibbi Abruzzini, and Jake Wieczorek
“Every one of our grants is annual and project-tied. We have no reserves and no core funding, which means that stability, where it exists, is only ever twelve months deep.”

That is how one civil society organization in Algeria described its finances to us in a recent survey. It is a sentence many donors would recognize from their own grant files, and it captures a reality familiar to many organizations: years of navigating short-term grants, restricted budgets and uncertain renewals, with little room to plan beyond the next funding cycle.

For years, civil society organizations have been encouraged to diversify their income, develop new partnerships and build financial and capacity resilience. But the latest — and many would argue the chronic — funding crisis is exposing the systemic retreat in development funding. Alternative sources are scarce, civic space is under pressure, and the political environment is becoming increasingly hostile.
A shock on top of a squeeze

Official development assistance fell by more than 23 percent in 2025, the largest annual drop ever recorded, and is projected to fall even more in 2026. Twenty-six of the 34 members of the OECD’s Development Assistance Committee cut their aid, and the US aid freeze that flooded headlines turned out to be just one part of a wider retreat.

To understand what this means in practice, the European Union System for an Enabling Environment for civil society (EU SEE) consortium partners — Hivos, Forus, Democracy Reporting International, European Partnership for Democracy, Transparency International and Civicus surveyed organizations in their networks between August and September, receiving 195 responses from over 68 countries.

The findings reveal the scale of the disruption: three-quarters of respondents say their funding is lower than at any point in the past decade. A third say more than half of their budget has been affected since January 2025, and 86 percent report harder terms, such as grants not being renewed, being reduced or cancelled or even more complicated compliance terms.

“The results show a perfect storm for civil society. Funding is disappearing at the very moment many organizations are facing greater political pressure. What’s being lost is not just programs and jobs, but the independent voices to defend rights, give voice to vulnerable communities, and hold power to account,” explains David Kode, program director of EU SEE.

The hardest hit were mid-sized, locally rooted organizations, despite having the most diversified funding. Among them, 90 percent reported funding cuts, 77 percent lost staff or reduced programs, two-thirds scaled back advocacy and community outreach, and 59 percent became less vocal publicly.
These are organizations connecting communities with services, donors and local governments.

Responses to question 11 in the survey: From January 2025 until today, what percentage of YOUR organization's budget has been impacted by donor budget cuts? Budget impact differs across organizational profiles. Screenshot from the survey. Fair use.
“We have had to sacrifice even our own salaries from other private sources to keep the NGO open and those who received a monthly salary are now working ad honorem,” said a respondent from Honduras.
In Indonesia, some organizations put staff on unpaid leave, while others could pay only half of their employees’ salaries.
What is lost beyond jobs

Yet the damage is not only monetary: almost half of respondents report reduced capacity for advocacy and about 40 percent say they have become less vocal or reduced their reach. A third of the respondents report having less control over their own priorities, and some have moved away from contested areas of work to keep their funding.

At the same time, almost two-thirds say civil society work has become less safe since early 2025, with more than half reporting more scrutiny, harassment or legal and administrative restrictions and half pointing to narratives portraying civil society as foreign-influenced.

This reflects a wider deterioration in the environment in which civil society operates. As one respondent from Zimbabwe put it: “The current funding crisis should not be viewed only as a financial challenge; it is fundamentally a civic space and democratic governance challenge.”

“An enabling environment is not simply the existence of a supportive policy. It is being able to register without unnecessary obstacles, access resources without compromising independence, speak and organise safely and meaningfully, influence decisions that affect communities — and knowing that when risks emerge, there are institutions and partners willing and able to respond,” says Marie L’Hostis, program and advocacy director at Forus.

These narratives do not stay rhetorical for long. The relationship between funding and civic space is particularly visible where governments are introducing or enforcing restrictions on organizations receiving resources from abroad.

In El Salvador, President Nayib Bukele accused journalists and civil society organizations of misusing USAID funds as part of a global money laundering operation, just as the US aid freeze hit. A few months later, the Legislative Assembly approved a Foreign Agents Law requiring anyone receiving funds from abroad to register and pay a 30 percent tax on those contributions.

By September 2025, long-standing organizations had begun to close: FESPAD, founded in 1988, and FUDECSO, after 33 years of work, both announced their dissolution, citing legal uncertainty and an unsustainable financial burden.

In Uganda, the proposed Protection of Sovereignty Bill 2026 would require any individual or organisation receiving money from outside the country, even from Ugandans living abroad, to register as a “foreign agent” and seek ministerial approval. In a country where most NGOs depend on foreign funding, that turns the loss of donor money into a question of legal survival. Foreign agents laws are spreading, stigmatizing civil society and choking the funding that remains.
The bigger picture

The consequences extend beyond the loss of individual projects. David Kode warned that the current crisis also involves “an erosion of relationships” and a breakdown of trust between donors and civil society.

A separate Forus report, “Strengthening the Enabling Environment for Civil Society: Evidence and Priorities for Action,” reaches a similar conclusion: abrupt funding shocks are not simply financial setbacks but structural threats to civil society’s independence and ability to act.
As report researcher Nicole Walshe put it during the launch, “without the resourcing, there is no civil society.”

The report points out that “these shocks transfer risk to local actors and weaken institutional capacity.” How long funding lasts, how restrictive its conditions are and who decides priorities all shape whether civil society can advocate, organize collectively and hold decision-makers to account.
So, what would make a difference?

Donors should protect continuity before disruption becomes irreversible: bridge funding, early warning of cuts and responsible exits. They should make compliance proportionate to context and risk, and fund legal, physical, and digital protection. The respondents call on national governments to protect access to domestic and foreign funding and the freedom to speak.

Governments can deepen the crisis or soften it. In Botswana, as international donors including USAID withdrew, the government reduced its own funding to civil society, including cutting all funding to the Botswana Council of Non-Governmental Organizations (BOCONGO), the national umbrella body. Organizations that support some of the country’s most vulnerable communities were left with neither international nor domestic support at the very moment both were needed most.

For Chris Nkwatsibwe of Uganda’s National NGO Forum (UNNGOF), civil society needs predictable, multi-institutional financing, alongside reserves that allow organizations to withstand political pressure and financial shocks. Domestic resources and alternative forms of ownership are equally important to reduce dependence on foreign funding and accusations of foreign influence.
“What kind of financing can now enable civil society to really genuinely remain independent, but also continue thriving in conditions of civic restrictions?” Nkwatsibwe asks.
The opportunity is to move from funding civil society to sharing power with it: in decisions, resources and defining success.
As Forus Co-Chair Moses Isooba told the Aid Matters 2026 conference in Vienna, “Power moves when three things change: who decides, who holds the resources and who defines success.”

In Morocco, Latifa Soufiani of Espace Associatif called on international donors and financial institutions to make respect for freedom of association central to their cooperation with governments. “We must be present to make our voices heard,” in international cooperation, she argued.

Luisa Rodríguez Táriba of Venezuela’s Sinergia highlighted how shrinking international support is undermining organizations’ ability to maintain teams and sustain both humanitarian and civic space work. As she observed, “The reduction of civic space doesn't happen overnight. It is multifactorial and happens over time.”

Despite the pressures, she offered a reminder that should remain at the centre of funding decisions: “The most important thing is people” and the communities they are part of must come before institutions, priorities and funding agendas.
