407f6f892ad9aeb7: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has designs for Cuba – and potentially on the U.S. presidency. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty ImagesThe so-called “blue tsunami” that hit the United States in the midterm elections is causing ripples around the world. Having won a historic victory, congressional Democrats now appear poised to challenge the Trump administration’s conduct of foreign affairs. The Iran war, support for Ukraine and the management of Venezuelan oil certainly all appear to be on the agenda of some Democrats. The flipping of the House and Senate from Republican to Democratic control has also led to speculation that members of Congress may also wish to challenge Trump’s Cuba policy. After all, the United States’ position on Cuba has swung in recent decades, depending on the balance of power in Washington. An easing of tensions and normalization of relations between the U.S. and Cuba took place under the presidency of Barack Obama, only to be reversed following the election of Donald Trump in 2016. President Joe Biden largely followed Trump’s lead, while making more allowance for activities supporting the Cuban people. In his second term, however, Trump has pursued an even harder line than before. Since January 2026, the administration has instituted a devastating economic and fuel blockade, prohibiting Cubans from importing oil. This pressure tactic is meant to get the Cuban government to agree to increased economic privatization and political democratization. A man walks in the dark during a blackout in Cuba on Sept. 18, 2026. AP Photo/Ramon Espinosa While the Cuban government has met certain demands, notably with respect to the economy, it has resolutely refused to change either its personnel or its authoritarian character. The result of this blockade has been a stalemate and increased hardship for Cubans. As a historian of U.S.-Cuban relations, I saw that hardship firsthand during a visit to Havana in June 2026. While I understand the notion that emboldened Democrats may try to force a change in direction of the Trump administration’s foreign policy, including on Cuba, I doubt they will be able to do so. In fact, there are reasons to believe that the midterm results may actually reinforce Republicans’ hard-line approach to the Caribbean island. Strained life in Cuba Since 1961, at the height of the Cold War, the U.S. government has enforced a rigorous sanctions regime against communist Cuba – the longest-running embargo in modern history. In January 2026, the Trump administration made that embargo even more severe with the oil importation ban, part of a regional pressure campaign that also saw U.S. forces abduct and remove from office Venezuela’s President Nicolás Maduro, a longtime ally of the Cuban government. For Cubans, no oil means no electricity. Blackouts, already a problem, have become longer and more frequent. Absent electricity, Cubans have no regular access to running water. Disease, from mosquitoes, other pests and unsafe water, has increased dramatically. Cuba’s once much-praised medical system often cannot treat patients unless they bring their own drugs and supplies. Inflation has soared and tourists have stopped coming, while industrial and agricultural production has declined dramatically. Cubans hate the U.S. embargo for contributing to this misery. At the same time, many also blame their government. During my last visit, Cubans I spoke with told me that they believe their leaders are more concerned with protecting their power and privileges than with the welfare of the average Cuban. For many Cubans, this indifference explains why President Miguel Díaz-Canel and his allies have rejected the Trump administration’s central demand of surrendering their monopoly on power. Havana’s strategy Trump’s demands, blockade and the threat of military force have led to some concessions by Cuba’s leaders. During the past year, Cuba’s government has released some political prisoners and permitted greater foreign investment, most notably from Cuban Americans. Blackouts are a part of life in Havana. Yamil Lage/AFP via Getty Images The government in Havana has also expanded the range of legally permitted private enterprise in Cuba. But when it comes to the question of power, Díaz-Canel and his allies remain implacable. They know that relinquishing power will cut off the supply of profits from state-owned businesses that flows their way and maintains their opulent lifestyles. They also argue that Trump has no right to determine the rulers of a sovereign nation. Rubio’s ideological priority For the moment, it appears that Díaz-Canel hopes international and domestic politics will compel Trump to turn his attention from Cuba. No doubt, the “blue wave” of the U.S. midterms has encouraged that belief. If so, I believe the hopes of the Cuban government are probably misplaced. This is in large part because U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a Cuban American who formerly represented Florida in the U.S. Senate, remains determined to topple the Cuban government. Rubio has long been a foreign policy hawk and fervent proponent of regime change in Cuba. As secretary of state, he has also been a key figure in the Trump administration’s push to expand American power across Latin America and support right-wing movements and governments. It is also no secret that Rubio wishes to succeed Trump as president. That has not changed since the midterm elections. In order to become the Republican nominee for president, Rubio will most likely need to win Florida’s primary. And if he is to win the White House, Rubio will surely need Florida’s electoral votes, especially in light of the results of last week’s election in Texas, which saw a U.S. Senate seat and the governorship turn Democrat. Rubio’s path to the presidency will be easier if he continues to enjoy the support of South Florida’s Cuban American community, which favors regime change by an overwhelming margin and represent a powerful voting bloc in Florida. In short, I believe ambition and ideology will provide Rubio with the impetus to refuse all compromise with what remains of Cuba’s communist government. Interestingly, some Republicans seem uneasy with aspects of America’s Cuba policy, particularly the emphasis on investment opportunities as opposed to democratic change. Nonetheless, Trump has reasons to push harder on Cuba. The midterm results show that his domestic agenda – and the war in Iran – are vote losers. He may see toppling the Cuban government as a guaranteed “win” for him and his administration, both in terms of legacy and in the eyes of voters. Congressional opposition? Of course, Democrats in the new Congress could deny the administration funds to maintain the oil blockade or, in an extreme case, invade Cuba. Democrats could also exercise Congress’ powers of investigation and oversight. Though these measures enjoy some support among Democrats, it is far from certain that House or Senate leaders would support them. After all, the Democratic Congress has other priorities that appear of greater concern to the American people, such as the Iran war, not to mention domestic policy issues, such as healthcare and an “affordability agenda.” Moreover, Democratic leaders may regard efforts to end the oil embargo as politically risky: Such efforts could alienate voters in Florida and divide the Democratic caucus, some of whose members favor the embargo. Outside of Florida, Americans generally disapprove of U.S. policy toward Cuba. But they are unlikely to demand that their representatives force the administration to change course. With the pressure on Democrats over Cuba relatively low, and their priorities elsewhere, the Trump administration will likely face little opposition to maintaining the embargo until it can say that it has achieved its political and strategic objectives. Meanwhile, members of Cuba’s governing elite, without appealing alternatives, will likely look to cling to power as long as they can. And the Cuban people will continue to pay the price. 9aba7fdcb091d85e: An order reissued by the Kuala Lumpur High Court led to two men packing their belongings and moving out — one out of prison, the other out of office.
The two are none other than former prime minister Najib Razak and now former transport minister Loke Siew Fook.

Now, Umno and maybe some PAS supporters are likely celebrating their “victory” — a conditional pardon for the former Umno president that sees him serving the remainder of his sentence under house arrest.
But can Umno really claim a “win” in this case?
If any party can hold its head up high in this affair, it certainly has to be Loke and DAP.
Loke stayed true to his principles, even if it cost him his ministerial post.
He vowed to resign if Najib set foot in the house and did not u-turn.
It is an admirable attribute, regardless of whatever side of the divide you are on.
Of all the adjectives available to describe Loke, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi chose “man of principle”, which must account for something, even if we were to doubt the deputy prime minister’s sincerity.

Loke’s resignation will help DAP recover its reputation as a principled party, especially among voters who have been disillusioned with them due to its partnership with Umno in the unity government and the administration’s delayed reforms.
Yes, being in bed with its most fiery rivals meant compromises had to be made for stability post-GE15, but the public doesn’t see it that way.
DAP, through Loke’s actions, may have also won over fence-sitters who are still angry with Najib and the 1MDB controversy.
Apart from these “wins”, unemployment may also work in Loke’s favour.
He now has the freedom to go to the ground to re-connect with the grassroots and members and he will be returning as a martyr of sorts.
Loke can now help revive the party in time for the 16th general election.
But what about Najib and Umno?
At the end of the day, Najib remains incarcerated — he only trades a jail cell for a comfortable home in Langgak Duta.
However, his movements, communication and personal contact remain restricted. To paraphrase a popular idiom: a cage by any other name reeks of imprisonment.
Secondly, Umno only managed to secure a conditional pardon and not a full one and helping Najib obtain a house arrest isn’t something one should boast about.
On top of that they had to help crowdfund RM50 million. Money that could have helped them win elections has been channeled to secure Najib’s house arrest.

Here’s the kicker. When the house arrest ends, he could head back to prison to serve his time for his 1MDB sentence, if he fails in his appeal. RM50 million would therefore end up being a hefty fee for a relatively short-term staycation.
Thirdly, Umno is now tasked with defending the indefensible and will have to do so with no moral ground to stand on, especially if they intend to play the religious card.

Umno, in this case, would have to answer for soliciting donations from people to help a convict who has yet to repent for his actions, which is religiously questionable and would likely haunt Umno in every election.
Umno’s friends and enemies will no doubt exploit this entire episode when jostling for seats during elections.
So. from where I stand, Loke and the DAP are the real winners here.
And all Umno has left is a house of cards.

c371d06a5231e17d: How do you think you're going to die?

If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US, it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week, Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident."

In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.
